questions.prompt: What does `stopImmediatePropagation()` do that `stopPropagation()` does not?

It stops only the capturing phase

questions.prompt: What is event bubbling?
key_points: The event first runs on the element where it happened, the target
Then it moves up through each parent, up to `document` and `window`
So parent listeners also run for events on their children
questions.correct_answer: Event bubbling means that after an event runs on the element where it happened, it travels up through every parent element to `document` and `window`. So a click on a button also triggers click listeners on its parent `div` and on `body`. This is what makes event delegation possible.

questions.prompt: What are the capturing and bubbling phases?
key_points: In the capturing phase, the event goes from `window` down to the target
Then comes the target phase, on the element itself
In the bubbling phase, the event goes back up from the target to `window`
Listeners run in the bubbling phase by default; `{ capture: true }` makes them run while capturing
questions.correct_answer: Every DOM event goes through three phases. In capturing, it travels from `window` down through the parents to the target. Then it runs on the target. Then, in bubbling, it travels back up through the parents. Most listeners run during bubbling; you pass `{ capture: true }` to `addEventListener` to run during capturing instead, for example to see an event before children handle it.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `stopPropagation` and `preventDefault`, and when do you use each?
key_points: `stopPropagation` stops the event from reaching other elements, but the default action still happens
`preventDefault` stops the browser's default action, but the event still bubbles
Example: `preventDefault` on a form submit you handle with JavaScript
Use `stopPropagation` sparingly, because it can break other code listening higher up, like analytics or delegated handlers
questions.correct_answer: `stopPropagation` stops the event from travelling further, so parent listeners do not run, but the browser still does its default action. `preventDefault` stops the default action, like submitting a form or following a link, but the event keeps bubbling. You use `preventDefault` all the time, for example on a form you submit with `fetch`. Use `stopPropagation` carefully: it also hides the event from delegated handlers and analytics code higher up the page.

questions.prompt: What is event delegation?
key_points: One listener on a common parent instead of one on each child
It works because events bubble up to the parent
`event.target` tells you which child the event came from
questions.correct_answer: Event delegation means putting one listener on a parent element instead of a listener on every child. It works because events bubble: a click on any `li` reaches the `ul`. Inside the listener, `event.target`, often with `closest`, tells you which child was actually clicked.

questions.prompt: Why is event delegation efficient?
key_points: Fewer listeners means less memory and less setup work
It works automatically for elements added later
The logic lives in one place
It is especially useful for long lists and tables
questions.correct_answer: With delegation you add one listener instead of hundreds, which saves memory and setup time. Items added later need no new listeners, because their events bubble to the same parent. The handling code lives in one place, which makes it easier to change. This matters most for long lists, tables and anything rendered dynamically.

questions.prompt: How would you write a delegated click handler for a list, and what edge cases matter?
key_points: Add one listener on the `ul`
Use `event.target.closest("li")`, or a data attribute, to find the item
Check that the item exists and is inside this list

questions.correct_answer: Add a single click listener to the `ul`. In it, call `event.target.closest("li")` to find the item, because the click might land on an icon or text inside it, then read something like `li.dataset.id`. Return early if `closest` gives `null` or an item outside this list. Remember that events like `focus` do not bubble, so use `focusin`, and that a child calling `stopPropagation` will hide its clicks from your handler.

questions.prompt: What are the differences between `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and cookies?
key_points: `localStorage` stays until it is cleared and is shared across tabs
`sessionStorage` belongs to one tab and is cleared when the tab closes
Cookies are sent to the server with requests, are small (about 4 KB) and can have an expiry date
Web storage holds about 5 MB of strings and is only readable by JavaScript in the browser
questions.correct_answer: `localStorage` keeps data until you clear it, and every tab of the site shares it. `sessionStorage` is the same kind of store but belongs to one tab and is wiped when the tab closes. Both hold around 5 MB of strings and never leave the browser. Cookies are much smaller, about 4 KB, are sent to the server with every request, and can be given an expiry date and security flags.

questions.prompt: Where would you store a theme setting, a form draft and a login session?
key_points: A theme in `localStorage`, because it should last and is not sensitive
A form draft in `sessionStorage` or `localStorage`, depending on how long it should last
A login session in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure` cookie set by the server
Explains the choice by who needs to read it and how long it should live
questions.correct_answer: A theme goes in `localStorage`: it should survive restarts, and it does not matter if a script can read it. A form draft can go in `sessionStorage` if it only matters for this tab, or `localStorage` if it should survive closing the tab. A login session belongs in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure` cookie set by the server, because the server needs it on each request and page scripts should not be able to read it.

questions.prompt: Why are `HttpOnly` cookies safer than `localStorage` for auth tokens, and what risk do cookies bring?
key_points: A script injected through XSS can read anything in `localStorage`
An `HttpOnly` cookie cannot be read by JavaScript
`Secure` makes the cookie travel only over HTTPS
Because cookies are sent automatically, they bring a CSRF risk
Reduce CSRF with `SameSite` and CSRF tokens
questions.correct_answer: If an attacker manages to run a script on your page through XSS, that script can read `localStorage` and steal the token. An `HttpOnly` cookie is invisible to JavaScript, so it cannot be stolen that way, and `Secure` keeps it on HTTPS only. The trade-off is that the browser sends cookies automatically, so another site could trick the browser into making a logged-in request: that is CSRF. `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict`, plus CSRF tokens for forms, protects against it.

questions.prompt: What happens from typing a URL to seeing the page?

The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, and runs scripts

questions.correct_answer: The browser first looks up the domain with DNS to get the server's IP address. It opens a TCP connection, adds TLS for HTTPS, and sends an HTTP request; the server sends back HTML. The browser parses the HTML into the DOM, downloads and parses CSS into the CSSOM, and runs scripts. It combines DOM and CSSOM into a render tree, works out the layout, and paints the pixels on screen.

questions.prompt: What are reflow and repaint?
key_points: Reflow, or layout, works out the size and position of elements
It is triggered by changes to width, height, fonts or content, and is the more expensive one
Repaint redraws pixels for visual changes like colour, without new layout
`transform` and `opacity` can skip both and run in the compositing step
questions.correct_answer: Reflow, also called layout, is when the browser works out the size and position of elements. Changes to width, height, fonts or content cause it, and because one box can push others, it can be expensive. Repaint is when the browser redraws pixels without changing layout, for example after a colour change. Changes to `transform` and `opacity` can often skip both and be handled by the compositor, which is why they are best for animations.

questions.prompt: How do you keep animations and DOM updates fast?
key_points: Animate `transform` and `opacity` instead of `top`, `left` or `width`
Group DOM reads before writes to avoid layout thrashing
Use `requestAnimationFrame` for visual updates
Avoid large DOM changes at once; use virtualisation for long lists
Use `will-change` sparingly
questions.correct_answer: Animate `transform` and `opacity`, which can skip layout and paint, instead of `top`, `left` or `width`. Do all your DOM reads first and all your writes after, so the browser does not lay out again and again. Schedule visual updates with `requestAnimationFrame` so they line up with the screen refresh. Keep the DOM small: render long lists with virtualisation instead of thousands of rows. Use `will-change` only for elements that really animate.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `async` and `defer`?
key_points: Both download the script without blocking HTML parsing
`defer` runs the scripts after parsing, in document order

questions.correct_answer: Both attributes let the browser download the script while it keeps parsing the HTML. With `defer`, scripts run after the HTML is fully parsed, in the order they appear on the page. With `async`, each script runs the moment it finishes downloading, in whatever order that happens, and can briefly pause parsing while it runs.

questions.prompt: Which scripts would you load with `async`, which with `defer`, and which normally?
key_points: `defer` for your app scripts that need the DOM or run in a set order

A normal blocking script only for code that must run before the page shows, like setting the theme to avoid a flash

questions.correct_answer: Your own app scripts should use `defer`, because they usually need the full DOM and may depend on each other's order. questions.prompt: How do script loading choices affect page performance?
key_points: Blocking scripts in the `<head>` delay the first render
Large JavaScript keeps the main thread busy and delays interactivity

`preload` and `preconnect` can speed up critical resources
questions.correct_answer: A blocking script in the `<head>` stops parsing, so the user sees nothing until it has downloaded and run. Even deferred scripts cost time to parse and execute, keeping the main thread busy and making the page slow to respond. So load third-party scripts late, for example with Next.js `lazyOnload` or `afterInteractive`, and split your own code so each page loads only what it needs, using dynamic `import()` for rarely used parts. `preload` and `preconnect` hints can fetch critical files earlier.

key_points: `innerHTML` parses the string as HTML
User data can contain tags or event attributes that run code, which is XSS
`textContent` inserts plain text, so it is safe
If you really need HTML, sanitise it first, for example with DOMPurify
questions.correct_answer: `innerHTML` treats the string as HTML, so if it comes from a user, they can sneak in something like `` and run code in other people's browsers. That is cross-site scripting. `textContent` puts the string in as plain text, so tags show as text and nothing runs. If you truly need to show user HTML, clean it first with a sanitiser like DOMPurify.

questions.prompt: What does React do for you that you would otherwise do with DOM APIs?
key_points: You describe the UI from state, and React works out which DOM changes are needed
It batches updates to keep DOM work and reflows low
It handles events with delegation at the root
It escapes text by default, which protects against XSS
It keeps track of list items with keys, so it can reuse elements
questions.correct_answer: Without React you would select elements and change them by hand every time data changed. With React you describe what the UI should look like for the current state, and React works out the smallest set of DOM changes, batching them so the browser does less layout. It attaches event listeners once at the root and routes events for you. It escapes text in JSX automatically, so user data cannot inject HTML. And with keys, it knows which list items moved, so it reuses their elements.
